look_here_first: LOOK HERE FIRST: see the broad wheel of long, very slim radiating racemes on the flowering stem. Photograph the WHOLE head, then one branch and a mature spikelet. Many Chloris species make windmills, so the thin radiating silhouette alone supports a candidate, not a certain species ID; compare feather fingergrass and tumble windmillgrass.

learner_visual_status.note: Six physically verified images; five open-use license records. Ligule, fertile/sterile lemma, awn and scale-referenced spikelet still require original-pixel review. GitHub Pages publication unverified.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Compared with feather fingergrass, the existing slimspike photo shows relatively hair-thin, less obviously feathery rays. Tumble windmillgrass is particularly suggested by multiple vertically separated raceme tiers, not simply a large wheel. Species-level certainty requires mature spikelet and lemma details that this one source photo does not provide.

crew_field_walkthrough: Find the central point where slender fingerlike racemes radiate; the hand photo gives an approximate scale.
Trace one branch toward its tip and note spikelet rows along its length; this broad structure does not expose lemma/awn measurements.
Get the rooted crown, several mature whole heads, and one isolated spikelet at millimeter scale before distinguishing this from shortspike hybrid or tumble windmillgrass.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Full attached flowering head showing base-to-top raceme junctions with metric scale.
Face and side view of one mature unilateral raceme.
Dissected spikelet with fertile/sterile lemma and awns at millimeter scale.
Rooted flowering plant and blade/sheath ligule.
morphology_keys.field_photo_limitations: Species source determination remains provisional. Accepted name verified at POWO, but no independent botanical confirmation of this particular photograph; do not change county/range fields.
crew_field_steps: Trace the central junction where many slender rays spread outward; this arrangement is clearly visible in the current hand-scale image.
Compare the slender relatively open rays against C. virgata's fuller feathery terminal fan and C. verticillata's often separated tiers.
Finish with a ruler beside a mature spikelet, both fertile and sterile florets, and the awns. The saved image does not resolve that microanatomy.

field_id_measured_key_20261023.reference: Mexican Chloris taxonomic treatment and dichotomous key
field_id_measured_key_20261023.field_rule: In the treatment's perennial Chloris key, C. andropogonoides has one rudimentary floret, radiating racemes in one whorl and fewer than 10 spikelets per centimeter. The sterile lemma measures approximately 1–2 mm long and 0.3–0.5 mm wide. These are specimen measurements, not traits measured from current gallery photographs.
field_id_measured_key_20261023.compare: C. cucullata has racemes in multiple whorls and densely packed spikelets (>10/cm) in this key. C. virgata is keyed as an annual with a different sterile-lemma shape; do not separate on habit silhouette alone.
what_to_measure: Collect one attached mature raceme; record whether branches arise from one whorl or several
On a 1 cm segment of one mature raceme, count spikelets, using a millimeter scale
Under 10–20x magnification expose one mature spikelet and its single rudimentary floret
Photograph and measure the sterile lemma, expected 1–2 × 0.3–0.5 mm by this key
Photograph glumes, lowest fertile floret, awn insertion and the true ligule separately
field_id_measured_key_20261023.image_claims: No microscopic arrows added: the six GitHub JPEGs have not been inspected sufficiently to claim that sterile lemma measurements are visible.
